claims.text: Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exhibit gradual premelting.
Locally strained regions act as early melting nuclei in these nanoparticles.
Local chemical heterogeneity acts as an early melting nucleus.
High configurational complexity limits atomic mobility.
Limited mobility produces nanoscale composition fluctuations and strain accumulation.
Transient Cu-rich regions have lower cohesive energy.
Local compositional and strain heterogeneities lower the melting barrier and cause spatially inhomogeneous melting.
The starting Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are solid and homogeneous.
Atomic-size mismatch and limited diffusion cause small regions to become compositionally and structurally distinct.
Defect-rich regions have a lower melting point than the surrounding material and initiate premelting at lower temperatures.
Liquid-like zones spread gradually through a nanoparticle and broaden its melting transition.
Relative to comparable single-metal or binary nanoparticles, the HEA nanoparticles will begin premelting earlier.
Relative to comparable single-metal or binary nanoparticles, the HEA nanoparticles will undergo a more gradual and spatially distributed melting transition.
Diffraction-peak broadening and spatially localized melting patches will appear before complete melting.
Comparable single-metal or binary nanoparticles typically have sharper and more uniform melting transitions.
The proposed mechanism applies when heating is sufficiently rapid that atomic diffusion remains limited and atomic-size mismatch generates local strain.
Slow heating can permit equilibrium diffusion to remove or overcome local heterogeneities, making the mechanism inapplicable.
The comparison should use particles of similar size under identical heating rates and ambient conditions.

contradictions.description: The initial particles are described without qualification as homogeneous, while the proposed governing state includes pre-existing or developing nanoscale chemical heterogeneities. This could be reconciled by distinguishing macroscopically single-phase homogeneity from local compositional fluctuations, but that distinction is not stated.
